user_input: What's the recommended way to target a button by the label a user would read on it?
reference: Reach for a role locator such as page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }). Playwright pushes you toward role-based locators because they mirror how real users and assistive tech experience the page.
reference_contexts: We recommend prioritizing role locators to locate elements, as it is the closest way to how users and assistive technology perceive the page.
llm_response:
The recommended way to target a button by the label a user would read on it is to use `page.getByRole()`. 

You should prioritize role locators because they reflect how users and assistive technology perceive the page. When using this method, you should pass the button's role and its accessible name to pinpoint the exact element.

**Example:**
`await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();`

You can also use a regular expression for the name if needed:
`await page.getByRole('button', { name: /submit/i }).click();`

Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and
`beforeEach`
hooks is included in the test timeout.

`afterEach`
hooks, after the test function has finished.

The same timeout value also applies to
`beforeAll`
and
`afterAll`
hooks, but they do not share time with any test.

Playwright includes test assertions in the form of
`expect`

generic matchers (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-genericassertions)
like
`toEqual`

`toContain`

`expect(success).toBeTruthy();`


Playwright also includes web-specific

`awaitexpect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Submitted');`

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Test retries are a way to automatically re-run a test when it fails. This is useful when a test is flaky and fails intermittently. Test retries are configured in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

## Failures​ {#failures}

Playwright Test runs tests in worker processes. These processes are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

Consider the following snippet:


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe('suite',()=>{test.beforeAll(async()=>{/* ... */});test('first good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('second flaky',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('third good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test.afterAll(async()=>{/* ... */});});`


When
all tests pass
, they will run in order in the same worker process.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Test can record videos for your tests, controlled by the

`'off'`
- Do not record video.
`'on'`

`'retain-on-failure'`

`'on-first-retry'`

Video files will appear in the test output directory, typically
`test-results`

user_input: I pulled a trace.zip off CI — how do I actually open it on my machine?
reference: Hand it to the CLI: npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip.
reference_contexts: npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip
llm_response:
You can open your `trace.zip` file using one of the following two methods:

### 1. Using the Playwright CLI (Recommended)
Run the following command in your terminal, replacing `path/to/trace.zip` with the actual path to your file:

```bash
npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip
```

### 2. Using the browser-based Trace Viewer
You can use the statically hosted Trace Viewer at [trace.playwright.dev](https://trace.playwright.dev). Once on the site, you can open your trace by:
*   Dragging and dropping the `trace.zip` file into the browser window.
*   Clicking the **Select file** button to upload the file from your machine.

This method loads the trace entirely in your browser and does not transmit any data externally.

`npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip`


### Usingtrace.playwright.dev​ {#using-traceplaywrightdev}

trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev)
is a statically hosted variant of the Trace Viewer. You can upload a trace file using drag and drop or via the
`Select file`
button.

Trace Viewer loads the trace entirely in your browser and does not transmit any data externally.

### Viewing remote traces​ {#viewing-remote-traces}

You can open remote traces directly using its URL. This makes it easy to view the remote trace without having to manually download the file from CI runs, for example.


`npx playwright show-trace https://example.com/trace.zip`


When using
trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev)
, you can also pass the URL of your uploaded trace at some accessible storage (e.g. inside your CI) as a query parameter. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) rules might apply.

# Trace viewer | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/trace-viewer>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Trace Viewer is a GUI tool that helps you explore recorded Playwright traces after the script has run. Traces are a great way for debugging your tests when they fail on CI. You can open traces
locally (https://playwright.dev/docs/trace-viewer#opening-trace-viewer)
or in your browser on
trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev)
.

## Opening Trace Viewer​ {#opening-trace-viewer}

You can open a saved trace using either the Playwright CLI or in the browser at
trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev)
. Make sure to add the full path to where your
`trace.zip`
file is located.


`npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip`


### Usingtrace.playwright.dev​ {#using-traceplaywrightdev}

Traces are recorded using the new
browserContext.tracing (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-tracing)
API:


`constbrowser=awaitchromium.launch();constcontext=awaitbrowser.newContext();// Start tracing before creating / navigating a page.awaitcontext.tracing.start({screenshots:true,snapshots:true});constpage=awaitcontext.newPage();awaitpage.goto('https://playwright.dev');// Stop tracing and export it into a zip archive.awaitcontext.tracing.stop({path:'trace.zip'});`


Traces are examined later with the Playwright CLI:


`npx playwright show-trace trace.zip`


That will open the following GUI:

👉 Read more in
trace viewer documentation (https://playwright.dev/docs/trace-viewer)
.

#### Browser Versions​ {#browser-versions-44}

Chromium 93.0.4530.0
Mozilla Firefox 89.0
WebKit 14.2

This version of Playwright was also tested against the following stable channels:

Google Chrome 91
Microsoft Edge 91

#### New APIs​ {#new-apis-19}

`https://trace.playwright.dev/?trace=https://demo.playwright.dev/reports/todomvc/data/e6099cadf79aa753d5500aa9508f9d1dbd87b5ee.zip`


## Recording a trace​ {#recording-a-trace}

### Tracing locally​ {#tracing-locally}

To record a trace during development mode set the
`--trace`
flag to
`on`
when running your tests. You can also use
UI Mode (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-ui-mode)
for a better developer experience, as it traces each test automatically.


`npx playwrighttest--traceon`


You can then open the HTML report and click on the trace icon to open the trace.


`npx playwright show-report`


### Tracing on CI​ {#tracing-on-ci}

Traces should be run on continuous integration on the first retry of a failed test by setting the
`trace: 'on-first-retry'`
option in the test configuration file. This will produce a
`trace.zip`
file for each test that was retried.

Test
Library
playwright.config.ts

`npx playwright show-report`


## Opening the trace​ {#opening-the-trace}

In the HTML report, click on the trace icon next to the test file name to directly open the trace for the required test.

You can also click to open the detailed view of the test and scroll down to the
`'Traces'`
tab and open the trace by clicking on the trace screenshot.

To learn more about reporters, check out our detailed guide on reporters including the
HTML Reporter (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-reporters#html-reporter)
.

## Viewing the trace​ {#viewing-the-trace}

View traces of your test by clicking through each action or hovering using the timeline and see the state of the page before and after the action. Inspect the log, source and network, errors, and console during each step of the test. The trace viewer creates a DOM snapshot so you can fully interact with it and open the browser DevTools to inspect the HTML, CSS, etc.

To learn more about available options to record a trace check out our detailed guide on
Trace Viewer (https://playwright.dev/docs/trace-viewer)
.

Traces are normally run in a Continuous Integration (CI) environment, because locally you can use
UI Mode (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-ui-mode)
for developing and debugging tests. However, if you want to run traces locally without using
UI Mode (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-ui-mode)
, you can force tracing to be on with
`--trace on`
.


`npx playwrighttest--traceon`


## Opening the HTML report​ {#opening-the-html-report}

The HTML report shows you a report of all your tests that have been run and on which browsers as well as how long they took. Tests can be filtered by passed tests, failed, flaky, or skipped tests. You can also search for a particular test. Clicking on a test opens the detailed view where you can see more information on your tests such as the errors, the test steps, and the trace.


`npx playwright show-report`

## Recording a Trace​ {#recording-a-trace}

By default the
playwright.config (https://playwright.dev/docs/trace-viewer#tracing-on-ci)
file contains the configuration needed to create a
`trace.zip`

reference: Bound the parallel worker count with the --workers flag, e.g. npx playwright test --workers 4.
reference_contexts: npx playwright test --workers 4
llm_response:
You can cap the number of parallel workers from the command line using the `--workers` option or its shorthand `-j`.

You can specify the number of concurrent workers as follows:

*   **Using the flag:** `npx playwright test --workers=<number>`
*   **Using the shorthand:** `npx playwright test -j <number>`

For example, to limit execution to 4 workers, you can use:
`npx playwright test --workers=4`

To disable parallelism entirely, set the value to 1:
`npx playwright test --workers=1`
llm_references:
Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)
to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

## Limit workers​ {#limit-workers}

You can control the maximum number of parallel worker processes via
command line (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-cli)
or in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

`npx playwrighttest--workers4`


In the configuration file:

## Disable parallelism​ {#disable-parallelism}

You can disable any parallelism by allowing just a single worker at any time. Either set
`workers: 1`
option in the configuration file or pass
`--workers=1`
to the command line.


`npx playwrighttest--workers=1`

# Parallelism | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Test runs tests in parallel. In order to achieve that, it runs several worker processes that run at the same time. By default,
test files
are run in parallel. Tests in a single file are run in order, in the same worker process.

You can configure tests using

to run
tests in a single file
in parallel.

entire project
to have all tests in all files to run in parallel using

or
testConfig.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-fully-parallel)
.
To
disable

user_input: If my selector happens to match several elements and I try to click, what does Playwright do?
reference: It refuses to guess — locators are strict, so any action that needs one element throws when the locator resolves to more than one.
reference_contexts: Locators are strict. This means that all operations on locators that imply some target DOM element will throw an exception if more than one element matches. For example, the following call throws if there are several buttons in the DOM:
llm_response:
Because locators are strict, Playwright will throw an exception if you attempt to perform a `click()` on a locator that matches more than one element. Playwright requires the locator to resolve to exactly one element as part of its actionability checks before performing the click.

If you need to handle multiple elements, you can opt-out of strictness by using `locator.first()`, `locator.last()`, or `locator.nth()`, though the documentation notes that these methods are not recommended because they may lead to clicking unintended elements if the page changes. The recommended approach is to create a locator that uniquely identifies the target element.
llm_references:
The code inside
locator.evaluateAll() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-evaluate-all)
runs in the page, you can call any DOM apis there.


`constrows=page.getByRole('listitem');consttexts=awaitrows.evaluateAll(list=>list.map(element=>element.textContent));`


## Strictness​ {#strictness}

Locators are strict. This means that all operations on locators that imply some target DOM element will throw an exception if more than one element matches. For example, the following call throws if there are several buttons in the DOM:

#### Throws an error if more than one​ {#throws-an-error-if-more-than-one}


`awaitpage.getByRole('button').click();`


On the other hand, Playwright understands when you perform a multiple-element operation, so the following call works perfectly fine when the locator resolves to multiple elements.

#### Works fine with multiple elements​ {#works-fine-with-multiple-elements}


`awaitpage.getByRole('button').count();`

#### Works fine with multiple elements​ {#works-fine-with-multiple-elements}


`awaitpage.getByRole('button').count();`


You can explicitly opt-out from strictness check by telling Playwright which element to use when multiple elements match, through
locator.first() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-first)
,
locator.last() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-last)
, and
locator.nth() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-nth)
. These methods are
not recommended
because when your page changes, Playwright may click on an element you did not intend. Instead, follow best practices above to create a locator that uniquely identifies the target element.

## More Locators​ {#more-locators}

For less commonly used locators, look at the
other locators (https://playwright.dev/docs/other-locators)
guide.

user_input: How do I choose an option in a <select>, and can I pick several at once?
reference: Call selectOption() with the option's value or label; pass an array when you need multiple selected.
reference_contexts: Selects one or multiple options in the <select> element with locator.selectOption() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-select-option) . You can specify option value , or label to select. Multiple options can be selected.
llm_response:
To choose an option in a `<select>` element, use the `selectOption` method. You can select multiple options at once by passing an array of values to the method.

### How to choose options
You can select options by providing a string (which matches both the value and the label) or an object specifying the label:

*   **Single selection (by value or label):**
    `handle.selectOption('blue');`
*   **Single selection (by label):**
    `handle.selectOption({label: 'Blue'});`
*   **Multiple selection:**
    Pass an array of values to select multiple options:
    `handle.selectOption(['red', 'green', 'blue']);`

### Important details
*   **Multiple attribute:** If the `<select>` element has the `multiple` attribute, all matching options provided in the array will be selected. If the `multiple` attribute is not present, only the first option matching one of the passed options will be selected.
*   **Actionability:** The method performs actionability checks and waits until all specified options are present in the element before selecting them.
*   **Events:** Selecting options triggers `change` and `input` events.
*   **Validation:** The method throws an error if the target element is not a `<select>` element (unless it is inside a `<label>` with an associated control, in which case the control is used).

user_input: If my page throws up an alert or confirm and I never handle it, will my test get stuck?
reference: No — with no dialog listener registered, Playwright dismisses dialogs automatically, so they won't block the run.
reference_contexts: If there is no listener for page.on('dialog') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-dialog) , all dialogs are automatically dismissed.
llm_response:
No, your test will not get stuck. By default, Playwright automatically dismisses dialogs (such as `alert`, `confirm`, `prompt`, or `beforeunload`) if no `page.on('dialog')` or `browserContext.on('dialog')` listener is present.

However, if you do register a listener for the `dialog` event, you **must** explicitly call either `dialog.accept()` or `dialog.dismiss()`. If you register a listener but fail to perform one of these actions, the page will freeze and your test actions (such as `locator.click()`) will stall because the dialog blocks further page execution.

# Dialogs | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/dialogs>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright can interact with the web page dialogs such as
alert (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
,
confirm (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/confirm)
,
prompt (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/prompt)
as well as
beforeunload (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/beforeunload_event)
confirmation. For print dialogs, see
Print (https://playwright.dev/docs/dialogs#print-dialogs)
.

## alert(), confirm(), prompt() dialogs​ {#alert-confirm-prompt-dialogs}

By default, dialogs are auto-dismissed by Playwright, so you don't have to handle them. However, you can register a dialog handler before the action that triggers the dialog to either
dialog.accept() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-dialog#dialog-accept)
or
dialog.dismiss() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-dialog#dialog-dismiss)
it.

## beforeunload dialog​ {#beforeunload-dialog}

When
page.close() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-close)
is invoked with the truthy
runBeforeUnload (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-close-option-run-before-unload)
value, the page runs its unload handlers. This is the only case when
page.close() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-close)
does not wait for the page to actually close, because it might be that the page stays open in the end of the operation.

You can register a dialog handler to handle the
`beforeunload`
dialog yourself:


`page.on('dialog',asyncdialog=>{assert(dialog.type()==='beforeunload');awaitdialog.dismiss();});awaitpage.close({runBeforeUnload:true});`

Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.

Here is the simplest way to handle the file download:


`// Start waiting for download before clicking. Note no await.constdownloadPromise=page.waitForEvent('download');awaitpage.getByText('Download file').click();constdownload=awaitdownloadPromise;// Wait for the download process to complete and save the downloaded file somewhere.awaitdownload.saveAs('/path/to/save/at/'+download.suggestedFilename());`

If you have no idea what initiates the download, you can still handle the event:


`page.on('download',download=>download.path().then(console.log));`


Note that handling the event forks the control flow and makes the script harder to follow. Your scenario might end while you are downloading a file since your main control flow is not awaiting for this operation to resolve.

llm_response:
You should store authenticated browser state in the `playwright/.auth` directory.

To keep this state out of version control, you must add `playwright/.auth` to your `.gitignore` file. 

The documentation provides the following commands to create the directory and update `.gitignore` based on your environment:

*   **Bash:**
    `mkdir -p playwright/.auth`
    `echo $'\nplaywright/.auth' >> .gitignore`

*   **PowerShell:**
    `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path playwright\.auth`
    `Add-Content -Path .gitignore "`r`nplaywright/.auth"`

*   **Batch:**
    `md playwright\.auth`
    `echo. >> .gitignore`
    `echo "playwright/.auth" >> .gitignore`

Because the state files contain sensitive cookies and headers that could be used to impersonate you or your test account, you should never check them into public or private repositories.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright executes tests in isolated environments called
browser contexts (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures. Tests can load existing authenticated state. This eliminates the need to authenticate in every test and speeds up test execution.

user_input: How do I split my tests to run across several machines at once?
reference: Shard with --shard=x/y — run 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 on four machines so each takes a quarter of the suite.
reference_contexts:
npx playwright test --shard=1/4
npx playwright test --shard=2/4
npx playwright test --shard=3/4
npx playwright test --shard=4/4
llm_response:
To split your tests to run across several machines, you use the `--shard=x/y` command-line argument. For example, to split your suite into four shards, you would run the following commands on separate machines or CI jobs:

* `npx playwright test --shard=1/4`
* `npx playwright test --shard=2/4`
* `npx playwright test --shard=3/4`
* `npx playwright test --shard=4/4`

### Balancing Shards
The documentation recommends using `fullyParallel: true` in your configuration to ensure the most effective and balanced distribution of tests across shards. 

* **With `fullyParallel: true`**: Playwright splits tests at the individual test level, which is the preferred mode for ensuring even load distribution.
* **Without `fullyParallel`**: Playwright splits tests at the file level. To balance shards in this mode, you must manually keep your test files small and evenly sized to avoid imbalances.

### Merging Reports
Because each shard generates its own report, you can create a combined report by using the `blob` reporter.

1.  **Configure the reporter**: Add the `blob` reporter to your `playwright.config.ts` file:
    ```typescript
    export default defineConfig({
      testDir: './tests',
      reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',
    });
    ```
2.  **Merge the reports**: After the shards have finished, use the following command to merge the results into a single HTML report:
    `npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports`

# Sharding | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/test-sharding>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

By default, Playwright runs test files in
parallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
and strives for optimal utilization of CPU cores on your machine. In order to achieve even greater parallelisation, you can further scale Playwright test execution by running tests on multiple machines simultaneously. We call this mode of operation "sharding". Sharding in Playwright means splitting your tests into smaller parts called "shards". Each shard is like a separate job that can run independently. The whole purpose is to divide your tests to speed up test runtime.

When you shard your tests, each shard can run on its own, utilizing the available CPU cores. This helps speed up the testing process by doing tasks simultaneously.

When you shard your tests, each shard can run on its own, utilizing the available CPU cores. This helps speed up the testing process by doing tasks simultaneously.

In a CI pipeline, each shard can run as a separate job, making use of the hardware resources available in your CI pipeline, like CPU cores, to run tests faster.

## Sharding tests between multiple machines​ {#sharding-tests-between-multiple-machines}

To shard the test suite, pass
`--shard=x/y`
to the command line. For example, to split the suite into four shards, each running one fourth of the tests:


`npx playwrighttest--shard=1/4npx playwrighttest--shard=2/4npx playwrighttest--shard=3/4npx playwrighttest--shard=4/4`


Now, if you run these shards in parallel on different jobs, your test suite completes four times faster.

Now, if you run these shards in parallel on different jobs, your test suite completes four times faster.

Note that Playwright can only shard tests that can be run in parallel. By default, this means Playwright will shard test files. Learn about other options in the
parallelism guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
.

## Balancing Shards​ {#balancing-shards}

Sharding can be done at two levels of granularity depending on whether you use the
testProject.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-fully-parallel)
option or not. This affects how the tests are balanced across the shards.

Sharding with fullyParallel

Key Takeaways:

With
`fullyParallel: true`
: Tests are split at the individual test level, leading to more balanced shard execution.
Without
`fullyParallel`
: Tests are split at the file level, so to balance the shards, it's important to keep your test files small and evenly sized.
To ensure the most effective use of sharding, especially in CI environments, it is recommended to use
`fullyParallel: true`
when aiming for balanced distribution across shards. Otherwise, you may need to manually organize your test files to avoid imbalances.

## Merging reports from multiple shards​ {#merging-reports-from-multiple-shards}

In the previous example, each test shard has its own test report. If you want to have a combined report showing all the test results from all the shards, you can merge them.

Start with adding
`blob`
reporter to the config when running on CI:

playwright.config.ts

`exportdefaultdefineConfig({testDir:'./tests',reporter:process.env.CI?'blob':'html',});`

Sharding with fullyParallel

When
`fullyParallel: true`
is enabled, Playwright Test runs individual tests in parallel across multiple shards, ensuring each shard receives an even distribution of tests. This allows for test-level granularity, meaning each shard will attempt to balance the number of individual tests it runs. This is the preferred mode for ensuring even load distribution when sharding, as Playwright can optimize shard execution based on the total number of tests.

Sharding without fullyParallel

Sharding without fullyParallel

Without the fullyParallel setting, Playwright Test defaults to file-level granularity, meaning entire test files are assigned to shards (note that the same file may be assigned to different shards across different projects). In this case, the number of tests per file can greatly influence shard distribution. If your test files are not evenly sized (i.e., some files contain many more tests than others), certain shards may end up running significantly more tests, while others may run fewer or even none.

Key Takeaways:

`npx playwright merge-reports--reporterhtml ./all-blob-reports`


This will produce a standard HTML report into
`playwright-report`
directory.

## GitHub Actions example​ {#github-actions-example}

GitHub Actions supports
sharding tests between multiple jobs (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-jobs/using-a-matrix-for-your-jobs)
using the
jobs.<job_id>.strategy.matrix (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions#jobsjob_idstrategymatrix)
option. The
`matrix`
option will run a separate job for every possible combination of the provided options.

The following example shows you how to configure a job to run your tests on four machines in parallel and then merge the reports into a single report. Don't forget to add
`reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',`
to your
`playwright.config.ts`
file as in the example above.

user_input: How do I watch the browser as my script runs and slow it down enough to follow along?
reference: Launch non-headless and pace each step with slowMo — e.g. chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 }).

llm_response:
To watch your script run and slow it down, you can use the following approaches:

### To watch the browser
*   **UI Mode (Recommended):** Run your tests using `npx playwright test --ui`. This mode provides a better developer experience, allowing you to walk through each step and visually see what happens before, during, and after each step.
*   **Headed Mode:** Run your tests with the `--headed` flag (`npx playwright test --headed`) to open a visible browser window. Alternatively, you can set `headless: false` in your `playwright.config.ts` file or as a launch option.
*   **Playwright Sidebar:** If using the Playwright sidebar, you can enable the "Show Browser" option.

### To slow down execution
*   **`slowMo` option:** Use the `slowMo` option to slow down Playwright operations by a specified number of milliseconds. This is useful for following along while debugging.
    *   Example: `await chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 });`
*   **`page.pause()`:** You can insert `await page.pause();` into your script. This pauses execution and opens an overlay, allowing you to inspect selectors or perform manual steps. Note that this requires running in headed mode.

user_input: My e2e tests mutate shared server state and run in parallel. What auth model avoids collisions, and how do workers stay on separate accounts?
reference: Give each parallel worker its own account and authenticate it once with a worker-scoped fixture. Key the account on the worker's parallelIndex — which stays the same even when a worker restarts — so a worker always maps to the same account.
reference_contexts: This is the recommended approach for tests that modify server-side state . In Playwright, worker processes run in parallel. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once. All tests ran by worker are reusing the same authentication state. We will need multiple testing accounts, one per each parallel worker.

Each worker process is assigned two ids: a unique worker index that starts with 1, and a parallel index that is between 0 and workers - 1 . When a worker is restarted, for example after a failure, the new worker process has the same parallelIndex and a new workerIndex .
llm_response:
The recommended approach for tests that modify shared server-side state is to use **one account per parallel worker** [1].

### How to avoid collisions and stay on separate accounts:
To implement this, you must authenticate once per worker process using a unique account for each [1, 3]. You can achieve this by creating a `playwright/fixtures.ts` file that overrides the `storageState` fixture to authenticate once per worker [3].

1.  **Differentiate Workers:** Use `test.info().parallelIndex` (or `testInfo.workerIndex`) as a unique identifier to differentiate between workers [2, 3, 4].
2.  **Worker-Scoped Fixture:** Define a worker-scoped fixture (using `{scope: 'worker'}`) to handle the authentication [5, 6].
3.  **Unique Account Acquisition:** Within the fixture, use the unique worker identifier to acquire a specific account (either by creating a new one or selecting from a list of pre-created accounts) [2, 5].
4.  **Storage State:** Authenticate in a clean environment (by setting `storageState: undefined` when creating the page), perform the authentication request, and save the resulting storage state to a file path unique to that worker (e.g., `.auth/${id}.json`) [2, 5].
5.  **Reuse:** The worker will then reuse this specific authentication state for all tests it runs [1, 2].

Additionally, to isolate user data in the database, you can create a `dbUserName` fixture that uses `testInfo.workerIndex` to initialize a new user in the test database for each worker [4].

user_input: Two problems with how our team writes tests. The recorder is the fastest way for people to get started, but the selectors it emits break on the next refactor, and half our app is behind a login so recording anything past the sign-in page means clicking through the form by hand every single time. Are both of these things the recorder can be told to handle?
reference: Both are, and they're separate mechanisms. On selectors: the generator isn't emitting raw CSS by accident — it inspects the page and picks what it judges the best locator, prioritising role, text and test id locators in that order, and when a candidate matches several elements it refines it until it uniquely identifies the target. So brittle output is usually a signal about the markup rather than the tool: give the elements you care about a test id (or accessible roles and names) and the recorder will prefer those. You can also use Pick Locator to grab and hand-tune a single locator rather than recording a whole flow. On the login: record the authentication once with `npx playwright codegen <url> --save-storage=auth.json`, which writes the cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB state at the end of the session, then start every later recording with `npx playwright codegen --load-storage=auth.json <url>`, which restores that state so the app comes up already signed in and you record only the part you care about. That saved state is the same kind of artifact your suite consumes as storageState, so the recorded flow and the running tests can share it.
reference_contexts: Playwright will look at your page and figure out the best locator, prioritizing role, text and test id locators. If the generator finds multiple elements matching the locator, it will improve the locator to make it resilient that uniquely identifies the target element.
The test generator can also generate a test while preserving authenticated state.

Run codegen with --save-storage to save cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB data at the end of the session. This is useful to separately record an authentication step and reuse it later when recording more tests.

Run with --load-storage to consume the previously loaded storage from the auth.json. This way, all cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB data will be restored, bringing most web apps to the authenticated state without the need to login again. This means you can continue generating tests from the logged in state.
You can generate locators with the test generator.
llm_response:
Yes, the recorder can be used to address both of these issues.

**1. Handling fragile selectors**
The generator is designed to prioritize resilient locators, specifically role, text, and test id locators. If it finds multiple elements matching a locator, it automatically improves the locator to uniquely identify the target element, which helps reduce test failures and flakiness. You can also use the "Pick Locator" tool to manually generate and fine-tune locators to ensure they are robust before adding them to your code.

**2. Handling login requirements**
You can avoid manual login by preserving the authenticated state. You can perform authentication once, save the storage state (cookies, localStorage, and IndexedDB) to an `auth.json` file, and then run the generator with the `--load-storage` flag to consume that file. This restores the authenticated state, allowing you to continue generating tests from a logged-in session. Alternatively, you can use project dependencies to define a setup test that handles authentication before other tests run.

# Authentication | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/auth>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright executes tests in isolated environments called
browser contexts (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures. Tests can load existing authenticated state. This eliminates the need to authenticate in every test and speeds up test execution.

## Core concepts​ {#core-concepts}

Regardless of the authentication strategy you choose, you are likely to store authenticated browser state on the file system.

We recommend to create
`playwright/.auth`
directory and add it to your
`.gitignore`
. Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file in this
`playwright/.auth`
directory. Later on, tests will reuse this state and start already authenticated.

tests/example.spec.ts

`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test('test',async({page})=>{// page is authenticated});`


Note that you need to delete the stored state when it expires. If you don't need to keep the state between test runs, write the browser state under
testProject.outputDir (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-output-dir)
, which is automatically cleaned up before every test run.

### Authenticating in UI mode​ {#authenticating-in-ui-mode}

UI mode will not run the
`setup`
project by default to improve testing speed. We recommend to authenticate by manually running the
`auth.setup.ts`
from time to time, whenever existing authentication expires.

First
enable the setup project in the filters (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-ui-mode#filtering-tests)
, then click the triangle button next to
`auth.setup.ts`
file, and then disable the
`setup`
project in the filters again.

user_input: When I shard across CI jobs, how do workers, fullyParallel and retries interact to keep runs balanced and reliable?
reference: Inside each shard Playwright still runs worker processes; turning on fullyParallel shards at the individual-test level so each job gets an even slice rather than whole files. Keep retries enabled so that when a worker is torn down after a failure it simply restarts and re-runs the affected test.
reference_contexts: When fullyParallel: true is enabled, Playwright Test runs individual tests in parallel across multiple shards, ensuring each shard receives an even distribution of tests. This allows for test-level granularity, meaning each shard will attempt to balance the number of individual tests it runs.
Workers are always shutdown after a test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures) to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.
If you enable retries , second worker process will start by retrying the failed test and continue from there.
llm_response:
To balance and ensure reliability when sharding across CI jobs, these settings interact as follows:

**Balancing Shards (`fullyParallel`)**
*   **`fullyParallel: true` (Recommended):** Playwright splits tests at the individual test level, allowing it to distribute tests evenly across shards. This is the preferred method for achieving balanced load distribution.
*   **`fullyParallel: false` (Default):** Playwright splits tests at the file level. Shard balance depends on the size of your test files; if files are unevenly sized, some shards may run significantly more tests than others. To balance shards in this mode, you must manually organize your test files to be small and evenly sized.

**Reliability (`workers` and `retries`)**
*   **`workers`:** It is recommended to set `workers: 1` in CI environments to prioritize stability and reproducibility by running tests sequentially within each shard. If you have a powerful self-hosted CI system, you may enable parallel tests within a shard, but sharding across multiple CI jobs is the recommended approach for wider parallelization.
*   **`retries`:** When retries are enabled, if a test fails, Playwright discards the current worker process and starts a new one. A second worker process will then retry the failed test and continue with the remaining tests. This ensures that failing tests do not affect healthy ones and allows for recovery from transient failures.

**Interaction Summary**
By using `fullyParallel: true`, you ensure that the workload is distributed evenly across your CI jobs. By setting `workers: 1` in CI, you ensure that each shard remains stable and reproducible. If a failure occurs within a shard, the `retries` mechanism ensures the test is re-run in a fresh worker process, maintaining the reliability of the overall test suite.

reference: Prefer project dependencies. Because a dependency is a real project that runs ahead of the others, it plugs into the runner properly — the setup shows up in the HTML report, is traced, and can use fixtures — whereas globalSetup misses some of that.
reference_contexts: This is the recommended approach, as it integrates better with the Playwright test runner: your HTML report will include the global setup, traces will be recorded, and fixtures can be used.

llm_response:
You should use **project dependencies** for one-time setup. It is the recommended approach because it integrates better with the Playwright test runner than the `globalSetup` config option.

**Why you should use project dependencies:**
*   **Feature Support:** Unlike `globalSetup`, project dependencies support Playwright fixtures, full trace recording, and standard config options (such as `headless` or `testIdAttribute`).
*   **Reporting:** Setup actions are shown as a separate project in the HTML report.
*   **Browser Management:** You can manage browsers via the `browser` fixture rather than manually via `browserType.launch()`.
*   **Parallelism and Retries:** These are supported via standard configuration.

**Comparison:**
While both methods run before tests, the `globalSetup` config option lacks the features listed above, does not show in the HTML report, and requires manual browser management. The documentation explicitly advises considering project dependencies instead of `globalSetup` to get full feature support.

reference: Whether a request is routable depends on who owns it. Once a service worker with a fetch handler is installed it sits between the page and the network: the page-owned request is served by the worker and never reaches the network, so it isn't routable, while the worker's own outbound request is a separate, service-worker-owned request that context routing does see. reference: Installing the npm package is not the same as provisioning a machine that can run browsers, and that's the gap. `npm ci` fetches the library; the browser binaries are downloaded separately, and those binaries need operating-system level libraries that a developer machine already has from everyday browser use and a bare Linux runner does not. So there are two things to install, and the combined step is `npx playwright install --with-deps`, which fetches the browsers and the OS dependencies together — that's exactly the step the recommended GitHub Actions workflow runs between `npm ci` and the test command. The alternative, and the more durable one if you also do visual comparison, is to run the job inside the official container image via `jobs.<job_id>.container`: it keeps the dependencies out of the host environment and gives you a consistent rendering environment, which matters because screenshots differ across platforms.

reference: Yes. Storage state is portable between an API request context and a browser context, so you can log in via the API, export the storageState, and create a browser context seeded with those cookies — and each such context stays isolated from the others.

Test Isolation is when each test is completely isolated from another test. Every test runs independently from any other test. This means that each test has its own local storage, session storage, cookies etc. Playwright achieves this using BrowserContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext) s which are equivalent to incognito-like profiles. llm_response:
Yes, you can authenticate through API calls and hand that session to a browser context. Storage state is interchangeable between `APIRequestContext` and `BrowserContext`.

You can achieve this using the following approaches:

### 1. Using a file to persist state (Recommended)
You can save the authenticated state to a file and then load it into a new browser context.
*   **Save the state:** Use `requestContext.storageState({path: 'state.json'})` after performing your login API call.
*   **Load the state:** Create a new browser context using `browser.newContext({storageState: 'state.json'})`.

### 2. Passing the state object directly
You can retrieve the storage state object directly from the request context and pass it to a new browser context without using a file:
```javascript
const storageState = await request.storageState();
const browserContext = await browser.newContext({ storageState });
```

### Important Considerations
*   **Scope:** This method covers cookie-based, local storage, and IndexedDB-based authentication.
*   **Session Storage:** Playwright does not provide a built-in API to persist session storage, as it is not persisted across page loads. If your application uses session storage for authentication, you must manually save and load it.
*   **Automation:** It is recommended to perform this authentication routine in a setup project and save the state to a `playwright/.auth` directory to reuse across tests.

user_input: Almost all of our tests stub the search endpoint so they're hermetic, and that's been great until the backend quietly renamed a field and every test stayed green while production broke. I want to keep most tests stubbed but have a couple that exercise the real endpoint and only override one flag in whatever comes back. Can the same interception mechanism do both, and what changes between them?
reference: Both go through the same route handler; what differs is whether you ever let the request reach the network. A hermetic stub never does: page.route(url, route => route.fulfill({ json: ... })) answers from the test and the server is never contacted, which is why a server-side shape change can't fail it. To modify a real response you have to fetch it first — inside the handler call `const response = await route.fetch()`, read the real body with `await response.json()`, mutate the field you care about, and then fulfill with the edited payload: `await route.fulfill({ response, json })`. That gives you the real contract for everything you didn't touch, so the renamed field would have surfaced. Routes are matched most-recently-registered first and are scoped to the page or context they were registered on, so a spec-level `page.route` override can sit on top of a project-wide stub. If you want the real traffic recorded once and replayed thereafter, that's what HAR replay is for.

### fallback​ {#route-fallback}

Added in: v1.23

route.fallback

Continues route's request with optional overrides. The method is similar to
route.continue() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-route#route-continue)
with the difference that other matching handlers will be invoked before sending the request.

Usage

When several routes match the given pattern, they run in the order opposite to their registration. That way the last registered route can always override all the previous ones. In the example below, request will be handled by the bottom-most handler first, then it'll fall back to the previous one and in the end will be aborted by the first registered route.


`awaitpage.route('**/*',asyncroute=>{// Runs last.awaitroute.abort();});awaitpage.route('**/*',asyncroute=>{// Runs second.awaitroute.fallback();});awaitpage.route('**/*',asyncroute=>{// Runs first.awaitroute.fallback();});`

user_input: How does device emulation (viewport, user agent, touch) get applied per test, and why doesn't it bleed into other tests?
reference: Device parameters come from Playwright's device registry and are applied at the browser-context level. Since every test runs in its own isolated context — which can also carry mobile emulation, permissions, locale and color scheme — the emulation stays scoped to that test.
reference_contexts: Playwright comes with a registry of device parameters (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright-core/src/server/deviceDescriptorsSource.json) using playwright.devices (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-playwright#playwright-devices) for selected desktop, tablet and mobile devices. It can be used to simulate browser behavior for a specific device such as user agent, screen size, viewport and if it has touch enabled. All tests will run with the specified device parameters.

Browser contexts can also be used to emulate multi-page scenarios involving mobile devices, permissions, locale and color scheme. Check out our Emulation (https://playwright.dev/docs/emulation) guide for more details.
llm_response:
Device emulation is applied by configuring device parameters (such as `userAgent`, `viewport`, and `hasTouch`) either globally in `playwright.config.ts` within the `use` object, or for specific tests/blocks using `test.use()` or by passing the parameters directly to `browser.newContext()`.

Emulation does not bleed into other tests because Playwright achieves test isolation through **Browser Contexts**. Each test is assigned its own unique Browser Context, which is created specifically for that test. Because emulation settings are applied to these individual contexts, they remain isolated from other tests.

user_input: Our CI machines are a lot slower than our laptops and I've been sprinkling per-assertion timeouts around to get the suite green, which is clearly the wrong shape. Some tests now fail with a message about the test itself rather than the assertion, and raising the assertion timeout further doesn't help those at all. How many separate budgets am I actually dealing with, and which one do I raise?
reference: Three budgets, nested, which is why raising the wrong one does nothing. The test timeout is 30 seconds by default and covers the whole test — the test function plus fixture setup plus beforeEach hooks — and it's what you're hitting when the failure names the test rather than an assertion; raise it in the config's `timeout`, or per test with test.setTimeout(120_000), or test.slow() to triple the default. Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() have their own separate 5-second expect timeout, which is unrelated to the test timeout and is the one reported in a 'expect.toHaveText with timeout 5000ms' call log; set it globally with `expect: { timeout: 10_000 }` or per assertion with a { timeout } option. Because the assertion budget is consumed inside the test budget, pushing the expect timeout above the test timeout accomplishes nothing — the test dies first. beforeAll/afterAll get their own timeout, equal to the test timeout by default and adjustable inside the hook. The right fix for a uniformly slower machine is the config-level defaults, not per-assertion overrides.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and beforeEach hooks is included in the test timeout.
Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() have a separate timeout, 5 seconds by default. Assertion timeout is unrelated to the test timeout.
export default defineConfig({ expect: { timeout: 10_000, }, });
test('very slow test', async ({ page }) => { test.setTimeout(120_000); }); test.slow(); // Easy way to triple the default timeout
beforeAll and afterAll hooks have a separate timeout, by default equal to test timeout. You can change it separately for each hook by calling testInfo.setTimeout() inside the hook.
llm_response:
You are dealing with three separate budgets:

1.  **Assertion timeout:** This applies to auto-retrying assertions (e.g., `expect(locator).toHaveText()`). It is unrelated to the test timeout and defaults to 5 seconds.
2.  **Test timeout:** This is the budget for the individual test, including its `beforeEach` and `afterEach` hooks.
3.  **Global timeout:** This is the budget for the entire test suite run.

Since you mentioned that raising the assertion timeout does not help when tests fail with a message about the test itself, you are hitting the **test timeout**.

To address this, you should raise the **test timeout** rather than the assertion timeout. You can do this in several ways:

*   **For a single test:** Use `test.setTimeout(ms)` inside the test body.
*   **For a group of tests:** Use `test.slow()` to triple the default timeout.
*   **For hooks:** Use `testInfo.setTimeout()` within a `beforeEach` hook to extend the timeout for all tests running that hook.
*   **Globally:** Use `testConfig.timeout` in your `playwright.config.ts` file.

user_input: What's the reliable way to select a parent row based on a child element, and why avoid xpath=.. for it?
reference: Filter the parent by the child locator — e.g. getByRole('listitem').filter({ has: child }) — which is evaluated relative to the parent match. xpath=.. works but is brittle: any DOM change can break it, so prefer filtering.
reference_contexts: The filtering locator must be relative to the original locator and is queried starting with the original locator match, not the document root.

Alternatively, if you cannot find a suitable locator for the parent element, use xpath=.. . Note that this method is not as reliable, because any changes to the DOM structure will break your tests. Prefer locator.filter() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-filter) when possible.
llm_response:
The reliable way to select a parent row based on a child element is to use `locator.filter()`. You should pass the child locator to the `has` option of the parent locator.

For example, to select an `<li>` parent containing a label with the text "Hello":

```javascript
const child = page.getByText('Hello');
const parent = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({has: child});
```

You should avoid `xpath=..` for the following reasons:
* **Reliability:** It is not as reliable because any changes to the DOM structure will break your tests.
* **Implementation coupling:** XPath is tied to the page's implementation, whereas `locator.filter()` allows you to prioritize user-visible locators like accessible roles or text.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Large test suites can be structured to optimize ease of authoring and maintenance. Page object models are one such approach to structure your test suite.

A page object represents a part of your web application. An e-commerce web application might have a home page, a listings page and a checkout page. Each of them can be represented by page object models.

Page objects
simplify authoring
by creating a higher-level API which suits your application and
simplify maintenance
by capturing element selectors in one place and create reusable code to avoid repetition.

user_input: Before a click, what does Playwright verify, and how does that relate to the waiting a plain click already does?
reference: A click runs actionability checks — attached, visible, stable, receives pointer events, enabled — and auto-waits for them. The pointer methods bake that same sequence in (down to scrolling into view), so you rarely need explicit waits.
reference_contexts: Playwright performs a range of actionability checks on the elements before making actions to ensure these actions behave as expected. It auto-waits for all the relevant checks to pass and only then performs the requested action. If the required checks do not pass within the given timeout , action fails with the TimeoutError .
wait for element with given selector to be in DOM
llm_response:
Before performing a click, Playwright verifies the following actionability checks:

*   **Resolution:** The locator resolves to exactly one element.
*   **Visibility:** The element is visible.
*   **Stability:** The element is stable (not animating or has completed its animation).
*   **Event Reception:** The element receives events (it is not obscured by other elements).
*   **Enabled State:** The element is enabled.

These checks are part of the "auto-waiting" mechanism. Playwright automatically waits for all these relevant checks to pass before performing the click. If these checks do not pass within the specified `timeout`, the action fails with a `TimeoutError`. 

This auto-waiting is built into the click action itself, meaning you do not need to add manual waits for the element to become available or actionable. You can bypass these non-essential actionability checks by using the `force` option, though doing so will disable checks such as verifying that the element receives click events.

user_input: Where do downloaded files go, and why might they disappear before I can use them?
reference: Downloaded files sit in a temporary folder and belong to whichever context fetched them, so they vanish the instant that context is torn down. Each test gets a freshly created context, so grab anything you need before the test ends.
reference_contexts: Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.
Playwright uses browser contexts to achieve Test Isolation. Each test has its own Browser Context. Running the test creates a new browser context each time.
llm_response:
Downloaded files are stored in a temporary folder by default. You can specify a custom directory for these files by using the `downloadsPath` option in `browserType.launch()`.

Downloaded files may disappear before you can use them because they are automatically deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed. Additionally, if you handle the download event without awaiting the operation, your script might finish and close the context while the download is still in progress.

To persist a file, you should use the `download.saveAs()` method to copy the download to a user-specified path.

user_input: My manually-created context never produced a video file. How is video capture tied to the context lifecycle?
reference: Video is flushed when the browser context closes. With the test runner that happens automatically, but if you created the context yourself you must await context.close(), or the file won't be written.
reference_contexts: Videos are saved upon browser context (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts) closure at the end of a test. If you create a browser context manually, make sure to await browserContext.close() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-close) .
When using Playwright as a Test Runner, browser contexts are created by default. Otherwise, you can create browser contexts manually.
llm_response:
Video capture is tied to the browser context lifecycle because video files are only flushed, saved, and guaranteed to be written to the filesystem upon the closure of the browser context.

If you create a browser context manually, you must explicitly call `await browserContext.close()` to ensure the video is saved. Failing to await this closure prevents the artifacts from being fully flushed. 

Additionally, note the following regarding video availability:
*   The video file is only available after the page or browser context is closed.
*   If you use `video.saveAs(path)`, this method will wait until the page is closed and the video is fully saved before completing.

user_input: We rolled our own visual checks: capture a PNG, compare it byte-for-byte with a committed file, fail on any difference. It's unusable — it fails on the first run of any new test, it fails constantly on CI with what look like anti-aliasing differences, and there's no way to accept a legitimate design change short of regenerating files by hand. What does the built-in comparison do differently at each of those three points?
reference: Each of your three problems is a thing the built-in assertion already handles, because capturing an image and asserting on one are different operations. page.screenshot() just returns a buffer; expect(page).toHaveScreenshot() is a full comparison assertion. On first run there is no baseline, so instead of failing meaninglessly it takes screenshots until two consecutive ones match — which also settles animation and rendering noise — saves the result as the reference and reports that it wrote it; you commit that file. On CI, the baseline is keyed by environment: the snapshot name like example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png encodes the browser and platform (the project name replaces the browser when you use multiple projects) precisely because rendering, fonts and anti-aliasing differ across platforms, so Linux CI compares against its own baseline rather than your macOS one. And byte-exactness isn't required: `maxDiffPixels` (per assertion or globally under `expect: { toHaveScreenshot: ... }`) sets an allowance. When a change is intentional you re-baseline with `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` rather than editing files.
reference_contexts: Error: A snapshot doesn't exist at example.spec.ts-snapshots/example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png, writing actual.

chromium-darwin - the browser name and the platform. Screenshots differ between browsers and platforms due to different rendering, fonts and more, so you will need different snapshots for them. If you use multiple projects in your configuration file, project name will be used instead of chromium.
Sometimes you need to update the reference screenshot, for example when the page has changed. Do this with the --update-snapshots flag. npx playwright test --update-snapshots
export default defineConfig({ expect: { toHaveScreenshot: { maxDiffPixels: 100 }, }, });
llm_response:
The built-in `toHaveScreenshot()` method addresses your three issues as follows:

*   **Failing on the first run:** Instead of failing, Playwright automatically generates the reference ("golden") screenshot on the first execution. It captures multiple screenshots until two consecutive ones match to ensure stability, then saves the final result to the file system for you to commit.
*   **Failing on CI due to minor differences (e.g., anti-aliasing):** Playwright uses the `pixelmatch` library, which allows you to configure tolerance for differences. You can use options like `maxDiffPixels` (to allow a specific number of differing pixels) or `threshold` (to configure the image matching sensitivity) to prevent tests from failing due to insignificant rendering variations.
*   **Accepting legitimate design changes:** You do not need to manually regenerate files. You can update your reference snapshots by running the test command with the `--update-snapshots` flag: `npx playwright test --update-snapshots`.

user_input: We added an automated accessibility scan to the suite and it's been green for months. This sprint a screen-reader user reported that our settings panel now reads its sections in the wrong order after a refactor that only moved markup around — and the scan didn't say a word about it. What class of problem is that scan actually able to catch, what would have caught the regression, and can both live in the same test?
reference: The scan and the regression are aimed at different things, which is why one sailed past the other. An automated scan — the documented approach uses the @axe-core/playwright package, where you await `new AxeBuilder({ page }).analyze()` and assert the returned `violations` array is empty — detects *rule* violations such as missing or invalid properties. It has no opinion about whether the structure is the one you intended, and the docs are explicit that many accessibility problems can only be found through manual testing, recommending a combination of automated scans, manual assessment and inclusive user testing. What your refactor changed was the shape of the accessibility tree, and that is what an aria snapshot pins: expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot() captures a YAML representation of the accessibility tree — the hierarchy of accessible elements with their roles, attributes, values and text, with indentation carrying the nesting — and fails when the current tree stops matching it. Order and nesting are part of that representation, so a moved section shows as a diff. The two compose: accessibility tests are ordinary tests, so you can put both in one spec or keep separate ones. Bear in mind the tradeoff the docs draw between the styles — targeted assertions check one specific condition and get verbose over complex structures, while snapshots capture whole-structure state and are best for outputs that rarely change shape, which also means they need deliberate re-baselining when a change is intentional.
reference_contexts: The following examples rely on the @axe-core/playwright package which adds support for running the axe accessibility testing engine as part of your Playwright tests.

In Playwright, aria snapshots provide a YAML representation of the accessibility tree of a page. These snapshots can be stored and compared later to verify if the page structure remains consistent or meets defined expectations.

The YAML format describes the hierarchical structure of accessible elements on the page, detailing roles, attributes, values, and text content. The structure follows a tree-like syntax, where each node represents an accessible element, and indentation indicates nested elements.
Snapshot testing is ideal for: UI testing of whole pages and components. Broad structural checks for complex UI components. Regression testing for outputs that rarely change structure.

The automated accessibility scan (using `@axe-core/playwright`) catches automatically detectable accessibility violations, such as poor color contrast, missing labels on UI controls and form elements, and interactive elements with duplicate IDs.

The regression you experienced—where sections are read in the wrong order—would have been caught by **Snapshot testing** using `toMatchAriaSnapshot`. Unlike the automated scan, snapshot testing is order-sensitive; it compares the current accessibility tree of the page against a predefined snapshot template, and the test fails if the order of elements in the page's accessibility tree does not match the order in the template.

Yes, both can live in the same test. Accessibility tests work like any other Playwright test, and you can integrate both accessibility scans (via `AxeBuilder.analyze()`) and accessibility assertions (via `toMatchAriaSnapshot`) into your existing test cases.

reference: Two boundaries are in play. First, to get at computed style you have to run code in the page: a locator resolves to elements but only exposes what the API models, so anything the API doesn't cover you obtain with evaluate. For the whole set at once use locator.evaluateAll(), whose callback receives the array of matching elements — e.g. `await page.locator('td.price').evaluateAll(els => els.map(e => getComputedStyle(e).textAlign))` — returning an ordinary array back into the test. Second, that callback executes in the browser, in a different context from your test file, so it cannot close over test variables; that's why your threshold was undefined rather than throwing at definition. Pass it explicitly as the second argument: `locator.evaluateAll((els, limit) => ..., limit)`. Whatever you return has to be serializable to cross back — return the strings or numbers you want to assert on, not DOM nodes.

llm_response:
To assert that every row in your pricing table renders with a right-aligned computed style, you should use the built-in `toHaveCSS` assertion. This is the recommended approach for verifying computed CSS styles.

### Recommended Approach: `toHaveCSS`
You can use `toHaveCSS` to check the computed style of a locator. For example:

```javascript
const rows = page.locator('.pricing-table-row');
await expect(rows).toHaveCSS('text-align', 'right');
```

This assertion automatically handles retries and resolves the computed style for the element.

### Addressing the "Undefined" Issue
You mentioned that your previous attempt to reach into the page resulted in `undefined` when comparing against a variable. This occurs because Playwright test scripts and page scripts run in different environments. You cannot access test variables directly inside an `evaluate` function.

If you need to perform custom logic using `evaluate` (e.g., if you were manually checking styles), you must pass your variables explicitly as arguments to the function:

```javascript
const threshold = 100; // Your variable defined in the test

const isAligned = await locator.evaluate((element, thresholdValue) => {
  const style = window.getComputedStyle(element);
  return style.textAlign === 'right';
}, threshold); // Pass the variable explicitly here
```

**Summary of requirements:**
*   **Use `toHaveCSS`** as the primary, built-in method for checking computed styles.
*   **Pass variables explicitly** if you use `evaluate` to avoid the "undefined" environment issue, as variables from your test environment are not automatically available in the browser context.

user_input: I want to parameterize the same tests with different values — both at the test level and across environments. How do these two levels differ?
reference: You can parameterize at the test level or the project level. Project-level parameterization uses option fixtures whose values you set in each project's config, which is how you run the same tests against different environments.
reference_contexts: You can either parameterize tests on a test level or on a project level.

Playwright Test supports running multiple test projects that can be configured separately. You can use "option" fixtures to make your configuration options declarative and type safe. Learn more about parameterizing tests (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parameterize) .
llm_response:
Parameterizing tests at the test level and the project level differ in their implementation and scope:

**Test-level parameterization**
*   **Implementation:** You use a `forEach` loop within your test file to iterate over an array of data. You can apply this to individual `test()` calls or wrap them in `test.describe()` blocks.
*   **Scope:** This is used to run the same test logic multiple times with different data inputs (e.g., different names or expected values) within a single test file.

**Project-level parameterization**
*   **Implementation:** You configure projects in the `playwright.config.ts` file. This involves defining options (using `base.extend` with `{ option: true }`) and setting those values within the `projects` array in your configuration. These options can then be accessed in tests via fixtures.
*   **Scope:** This is used to run groups of tests under different configurations. It allows you to run the same tests against different environments (e.g., staging vs. production), with different settings (e.g., different timeouts or retries), or in different states (e.g., logged-in vs. logged-out).

One spec in our checkout suite never finishes — the runner sits on it until the whole run is killed. It's the test that exercises the 'delete saved card' button, which is the only place in the app that asks the user to confirm before proceeding. I added a listener so I could log what the prompt says, and the message does get printed, so it's not that we're missing the event. reference: The dialog listener must actually handle the dialog by calling dialog.accept() or dialog.dismiss(); otherwise the action stalls because dialogs are modals that block page execution. Fix by accepting/dismissing, e.g. page.on('dialog', dialog => dialog.accept()).
reference_contexts: page.on('dialog') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-dialog) listener must handle the dialog. A colleague added visual coverage to the checkout page and CI went red on the very first run of the new test — before anyone had changed any styling. The message doesn't read like a normal assertion failure and there's no diff image in the report, just this:

await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot();

Error: A snapshot doesn't exist at example.spec.ts-snapshots/example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png, writing actual.

Re-running the job locally doesn't produce the error. Is the test wrong, or is CI wrong?
reference: No. On first execution there is no golden file yet, so Playwright takes screenshots until two consecutive ones match, saves the last as the reference, and reports this message. The generated snapshot is ready to be committed; subsequent runs compare against it.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test includes the ability to produce and visually compare screenshots using await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot() . On first execution, Playwright test will generate reference screenshots. Subsequent runs will compare against the reference.
Error: A snapshot doesn't exist at example.spec.ts-snapshots/example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png, writing actual.

That's because there was no golden file yet. This method took a bunch of screenshots until two consecutive screenshots matched, and saved the last screenshot to file system. It is now ready to be added to the repository.
llm_response:
Neither the test nor CI is necessarily "wrong." The error message indicates that the golden (reference) snapshot file does not exist in the repository, which is expected behavior when running a visual test for the first time.

The reason you see this error in CI but not locally is due to how Playwright handles snapshot generation:

*   **Environment Sensitivity:** Browser rendering varies based on factors including the host OS, platform, and hardware. Because the snapshot name includes the platform (e.g., `chromium-darwin`), a snapshot generated on your local machine cannot be used by CI if the CI environment is different (e.g., Linux vs. macOS).
*   **Missing Golden Files:** When you run the test for the first time, Playwright generates the "actual" screenshot but fails because there is no "golden" file to compare it against. You must commit the generated snapshot file to your repository so that it serves as the baseline for future runs.
*   **Consistency Requirement:** For consistent screenshots, you must run tests in the same environment where the baseline screenshots were generated.

**To resolve this:**
1.  Ensure the snapshot file generated by the test (located in the `example.spec.ts-snapshots` directory) is added to your repository.
2.  If the CI environment differs from your local machine, you may need to generate and commit the snapshots specifically for that CI environment's platform and browser configuration.

llm_response:
The top-level element matches because `:has-text("Playwright")` matches any element that contains the specified text, including the `<body>` tag which contains all text on the page.

To narrow this to the specific element you want, you should use a more specific locator that identifies the container of the text rather than searching the entire document. The documentation recommends the following approaches:

*   **Scope the locator to a specific element:** Instead of searching the whole page, prefix the text filter with a specific tag or selector. For example:
    `await page.locator('article:has-text("Playwright")').click();`
*   **Use `hasText` option:** You can pass the text as an option to a locator:
    `await page.locator('x-details', { hasText: 'Details' }).click();`
*   **Use unique identifiers:** If possible, use a test ID to uniquely identify the element:
    `await page.getByTestId('orange').click();`

The documentation advises against using `nth()` or `first()`/`last()` to select from a list of matches, as these methods are not recommended and may point to the wrong element if the page structure changes. Instead, you should create a unique locator that satisfies strictness criteria.

reference: Mock Service Worker registers a service worker that grabs the traffic first, so Playwright's route() never sees it. Either set serviceWorkers to 'block' to remove that layer, or drop MSW and mock responses with Playwright's own routing.
reference_contexts: It might be that you are using a mock tool such as Mock Service Worker (MSW). While this tool works out of the box for mocking responses, it adds its own Service Worker that takes over the network requests, hence making them invisible to browserContext.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-route) and page.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-route) .

If you're using Playwright's native browserContext.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-route) and page.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-route) , and it appears network events are missing, disable Service Workers by setting serviceWorkers (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browser#browser-new-context-option-service-workers) to 'block' .

llm_response:
Targeted input actions, such as `fill()`, automatically distinguish between labels and controls, allowing them to perform actions on the associated input field even when the label is targeted.

However, `expect(locator).toHaveText()` does not share this behavior; it asserts the text content of the label itself rather than the value of the associated input field.

To fix this, you should use `locator.inputValue()` to retrieve the value of the input field for your assertion. Additionally, the documentation recommends locating by label text (using `page.getByLabel()`) rather than relying on label-to-control retargeting.

# Authentication | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/auth>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright executes tests in isolated environments called
browser contexts (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures. Tests can load existing authenticated state. This eliminates the need to authenticate in every test and speeds up test execution.

## Core concepts​ {#core-concepts}

Regardless of the authentication strategy you choose, you are likely to store authenticated browser state on the file system.

We recommend to create
`playwright/.auth`
directory and add it to your
`.gitignore`
. Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file in this
`playwright/.auth`
directory. Later on, tests will reuse this state and start already authenticated.

Specify
`globalSetup`
,
`baseURL`
and
`storageState`
in the configuration file.

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({globalSetup:require.resolve('./global-setup'),use:{baseURL:'http://localhost:3000/',storageState:'state.json',},});`


Tests start already authenticated because we specify
`storageState`
that was populated by global setup.


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test('test',async({page})=>{awaitpage.goto('/');// You are signed in!});`


You can make arbitrary data available in your tests from your global setup file by setting them as environment variables via
`process.env`
.

global-setup.ts

`importtype{FullConfig}from'@playwright/test';asyncfunctionglobalSetup(config:FullConfig){process.env.FOO='some data';// Or a more complicated data structure as JSON:process.env.BAR=JSON.stringify({some:'data'});}exportdefaultglobalSetup;`


Tests have access to the
`process.env`
properties set in the global setup.

After that, specify
`storageState`
for each test file or test group,
instead of
setting it in the config.

tests/example.spec.ts

`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.use({storageState:'playwright/.auth/admin.json'});test('admin test',async({page})=>{// page is authenticated as admin});test.describe(()=>{test.use({storageState:'playwright/.auth/user.json'});test('user test',async({page})=>{// page is authenticated as a user});});`


See also about
authenticating in the UI mode (https://playwright.dev/docs/auth#authenticating-in-ui-mode)
.
